summary: Proxy host-header rewrite causing route quota misattribution and unexpected 429s during multipart upload workflow
description:
Issue summary:
Customer StreamlineMaps on a Private deployment using an on-prem reverse proxy began receiving 429 throttles during a multipart file upload job that previously succeeded. The uploads are large (50–150MB per object) and the client uses parallel chunked PUTs with automatic retry. The customer reports the 429s started immediately after they enabled a proxy feature that rewrites the Host header to the internal service name for routing.

Impact:
- Production ingest pipeline experiencing intermittent failures for ~10% of objects during hourly backfills (affects downstream geodata freshness).
- Customer sees 429s with Retry-After headers; console shows available burst credits in the Private control plane.

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed control plane) in us-west region.
- Ingress: on-prem HA reverse proxy (envoy v1.25) rewriting Host header to internal-service.local for route affinity.
- Backfill worker fleet: 20 concurrent workers per host, HTTP/2 connection reuse enabled.

Steps to reproduce (provided by customer):
1) Enable Host header rewrite on their ingress so requests present internal-service.local as Host to the control plane.
2) Start the multipart uploader with 20 parallel chunk uploads per file, 500ms backoff retries on 5xx/429.
3) Observe a subset of chunk requests receive 429 responses; console credits do not reflect immediate exhaustion.

Observed behavior:
- 429 responses include throttle headers X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Window: route:short-window.
- Control plane metrics show token accounting against a route ID that does not match the customer's intended public route but matches the internal-service.local route assigned by the proxy.
- Retried chunks amplify the apparent per-route consumption, causing other tenants (on same private control plane) to see transient increases in their route-level counts.

Expected behavior:
- Host header rewrite should not change the tenant/route accounting; rate-limiter should use authenticated API key+path fingerprinting rather than Host header alone.

Attachments / Logs:
- Customer provided upstream proxy config snippet (sanitized).
- Excerpt of request/response pair (headers only) showing rewritten Host and throttle headers (attached to ticket).
- Control plane metric snapshot (token accounting per route) at time of incident (attached).
comments: 2026-03-10 09:15 UTC - Asha Raman (Support): Customer reports sudden chunk 429s after enabling host rewrite. Confirmed customer is on Private deployment; escalated to SRE for rate-accounting check.

2026-03-10 12:40 UTC - SRE (Liam O'Neal): Observed that route fingerprinting used by our rate-limiter includes Host header when request arrives via edge proxy. Running traffic replay locally against a staging rate-limiter to reproduce.

2026-03-11 07:22 UTC - Customer (StreamlineMaps - J. Park): Added that disabling host rewrite immediately stops 429s. We can toggle, but need a permanent fix because internal routing requires rewrite.

2026-03-11 15:05 UTC - SRE (Liam O'Neal): Applied temporary mitigation on customer's private control plane: added a request normalization rule that preserves original public host in the X-Forwarded-Host header and uses that for route-fingerprint. Early results: 2 hours of backfill with no 429s reported.

2026-03-12 10:03 UTC - Support (Asha Raman): Notified customer of mitigation and requested permission for a software patch rollout to change rate-limiter fingerprint priority to authenticated-key > path > X-Forwarded-Host > Host. Customer requested immediate patch rollout window 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC.

2026-03-12 14:12 UTC - Engineering (Marta Singh): Reviewing patch; finding a potential edge-case around HTTP/2 stream coalescing when X-Forwarded-Host is missing. Adding unit test to ensure we fallback to API key when header absent.
investigation_notes: Token accounting analysis: Several thousand chunk requests were attributed to route id 'internal-service.local' due to header rewrite. When requests reused persistent HTTP/2 streams, route attribution persisted across multiplexed streams and inflated the single-route counter.

Hypothesis: Rate-limiter currently builds route fingerprint from (Host, request-path, hashed-api-key) with Host taking precedence when present. Host rewrite changed which route was considered hot, causing misattribution.
Reproduction: Staging proxy replay with Host rewrite reproduced 429 pattern. Disabling Host rewrite or adding X-Forwarded-Host to preserved public host prevented misattribution.
Telemetry: No change in overall tenant quota usage shown in billing; discrepancy between per-route counters and tenant-level counters indicates counting at wrong aggregation key.
Risk assessment: High for private deployments with ingress rewrite features; moderate for hosted customers behind certain edge proxies that perform similar header rewrites.
resolution_notes: Mitigation applied: temporary request normalization rule configured on the customer's private control plane to trust X-Forwarded-Host when present and to prefer API key for fingerprinting. Engineering patch to adjust fingerprint precedence created (PR: https://github.com/redwood/ingress-proxy/pull/3284). Planned rollout: patch to private control plane images and a soft rollout on 2026-03-13 during low-traffic window. Follow-up: add defensive unit/integration tests for HTTP/2 multiplexed stream attribution and a runbook entry under Support for customers who use host-header rewrites.
next_steps: 2026-03-13 - Deploy patch to private control plane for this customer in scheduled window; monitor per-route counters for 24 hours.
Add integration test to CI that simulates host header rewrite + HTTP/2 multiplexing to prevent regressions.
Update public support KB: guidance on configuring on-prem ingress when using host rewrite and recommended headers (X-Forwarded-Host) to preserve route accounting.
Consider a long-term enhancement: change our rate-limiter to derive route fingerprint primarily from authenticated API key and request path, ignoring Host except as a last-resort tie-breaker.
